title: Who ran it, and who walked out
lede: Titles and dates follow the Times’s reporting and the filings cited; later careers are listed only where we found a source.

people.name: Nolan Bushnell
people.text: Founded Atari and commissioned Pong. Sold the company to Warner in 1976 and was removed by Warner’s Emanuel Gerard.[^1][^29]

people.name: Raymond E. Kassar
people.text: A 25-year veteran of Burlington Industries who tried to turn “a loosely organized band of engineers into a serious, businesslike, market-oriented company.” Sold 5,000 Warner shares on the day of the December 1982 warning. Resigned in July 1983.[^1][^2][^3]

people.name: Steven J. Ross
people.text: Built Warner from a funeral and parking business into an entertainment conglomerate, and disclosed the Atari insider sales himself in December 1982.[^2][^6]

people.name: Emanuel Gerard
people.text: Urged the 1976 purchase and later described the company as “blind-sided” by the cancellations.[^1]

people.name: James J. Morgan
people.text: Hired from Philip Morris at 41 with a contract reported to be worth more than $10 million. Learned of the sale to Tramiel days before it closed, according to an Atari executive.[^3][^7]

people.name: Jack Tramiel
people.text: Founder of Commodore, whose price war had hurt Atari. Bought the company for notes. He was named as a director of JTS in the 1996 merger plan.[^7][^11]

people.name: David Crane
people.text: One of four programmers who left in 1979 after being refused credit and royalties.[^26]
people.later: Activision was acquired by Microsoft in a deal valued at $68.7 billion.[^28]

people.name: Wade J. Rosen
people.text: Took over as chief executive from Frédéric Chesnais in April 2021. His company IRATA LLC is Atari SA’s reference shareholder.[^20][^21]
